content:
# Semantic-Anchored Checkpointing with Suffix-Only Re-Prefill — Edge Case Analysis

## The invariant everything hangs on

Cached KV for a span `S` may be reused across a context edit **iff**:

1. Token IDs in `S` are byte-identical to the previous version,
2. Absolute positions of `S` are identical (RoPE phase is baked into cached K/V),
3. Model fingerprint, quantization, and attention architecture are identical,
4. **No deletion has occurred upstream of `S`** since the cache was written (see FM-7 — this is the one people miss).

Everything else is re-prefill. Anchors exist to make the "unchanged?" check O(1) and to restrict edits to a safe grammar: **APPEND**, **TRUNCATE-to-anchor**, **AMEND-via-appended-correction**, **COMPACTION (delete + append summary)**, **FORK**. There is no IN-PLACE-WRITE primitive. In the Ledger of Empty Chairs terms: a sealed chair-entry or round-seal is an anchor candidate; tombstones and amendments are append-only by rule; the cache discipline enforces what the fiction already implies.

---

## Failure modes

**FM-1 — Anchor declared over mutable content.** Anchor placed at a point where later passes can still write (a chair-entry pending amendment, a turn awaiting a tool result). A later mutation invalidates the claimed prefix; if the engine trusts the declaration without verifying, it serves stale KV. Consequence: no crash — the model attends over values that don't match its visible context and produces confidently wrong, self-consistent hallucination. Worst severity class.

**FM-2 — Positional misalignment after insertion.** Inserting a block anywhere before an anchor (injected memory, a system reminder) shifts absolute positions of everything downstream. Cached K/V encode RoPE phases for the old positions. Naive reuse produces garbage attention scores — not subtle degradation, structural corruption. Corollary: "suffix-only re-prefill" is only valid when the suffix begins at the same position index as before. Length-changing edits kill every downstream anchor, period.

**FM-3 — KV resurrection across deletion.** Cached K/V for surviving tokens were computed by attending to now-deleted tokens. Even with perfect position remapping, the *values* latently encode the deleted content. In a ledger world this is the machine refusing to keep the chair empty: compacted-away events, scrubbed secrets, or retconned revelations persist in activations and leak into behavior. Any deletion boundary forces re-prefill from that point. No exceptions, no remapping exemption.

**FM-4 — Seam tokenization drift.** Prefix ends `…ch`, suffix begins `air`. Stored prefix tokenized as `["ch","air"]`; joint re-tokenization merges to `"chair"`. Divergence at the seam despite identical text. If the orchestrator splices raw token streams, corrupted text; if it compares text instead of token IDs, false misses. Rule: re-tokenize a window of the last ~8 prefix tokens joined with the first ~8 suffix tokens; walk the divergence point back as needed. Never detokenize the tail before continuing generation.

**FM-5 — Non-contiguous matching.** Divergence detection via LCS or similarity over messages instead of longest contiguous token-level prefix. Duplicate blocks (the same chair-inscription appearing twice) cause alignment off-by-N; LCS "matches" across gaps and claims reuse spanning an edit. Corruption, silently.

**FM-6 — Cross-branch cache collision.** Forking for parallel plans: if cache keys are `(session, position)` rather than content hashes, branch B reads branch A's pages. Contamination between counterfactuals — in a hidden-information game, branch A's private reasoning bleeds into branch B's decisions.

**FM-7 — Volatile fields updated in place.** The cumulative ledger digest or a "current tick" clock line rewritten each round/tick, sitting early in the context. Every update is a mid-context mutation → full re-prefill of nearly everything, every round, forever. This is the classic self-inflicted wound. Fix is structural: append per-round deltas; place volatile content as late as possible.

**FM-8 — Out-of-order tool assembly.** Multiple tool calls; results arrive out of order; assembly in arrival order differs from call order → mid-turn rewrite after the turn was provisionally sealed → cascade invalidation. Assemble deterministically in call order; never seal a turn until all expected results are present; late results append, never backfill.

**FM-9 — Sealing partial streams.** Anchor sealed on first chunk of a streamed tool result; remaining chunks land inside the sealed span. Appending into a sealed span is mutation. Either seal on stream completion or emit the remainder as a distinct appended block.

**FM-10 — Interrupted generation mishandled.** User interrupt leaves a truncated assistant turn. Sealing it, then replacing it later, is a mid-edit. Provisional turns are never anchored. Resume = append, or truncate-to-last-anchor and regenerate — truncation being the one destructive op that is free, since it preserves all upstream anchors and positions.

**FM-11 — Retcon temptation.** On a hidden-info reveal, retroactively redacting the secret from history. Destroys every downstream anchor *and* triggers FM-3 doubly: reused pre-redaction KV leaks the secret the redaction was meant to bury. Forward amendments only — which the fiction's own audit logic demands anyway.

**FM-12 — Entity-identity dedup.** A chair re-occupied by a returning entity matches an old span by actor ID; the system treats the return as "unchanged" and reuses stale context. Anchors key on event/span identity, never entity identity. An empty chair refilled is a new epoch, not a restored old one.

**FM-13 — Weak keys and version skew.** Cache keyed on short hash or (length, first-token) → collisions poison reuse. Missing model-version or precision tags → KV from a fine-tuned or requantized model served to another. 128-bit hash (BLAKE3-class) over token-ID sequence + position base + model fingerprint + precision tag; hard reject on tag mismatch.

**FM-14 — Precision mixing within a span.** Suffix prefilled fp16 attending over prefix pages downgraded to int8 under eviction pressure → nondeterministic quality dependent on eviction luck. Pin precision per session or downgrade whole spans atomically.

**FM-15 — Sampler state amnesia.** Repetition penalties, DRY windows, n-gram bans rebuilt only over the re-prefilled suffix instead of the full logical context. Penalties fire against nothing or against stale windows. Sampler state is always rebuilt from the full context, independent of KV reuse.

**FM-16 — Presentation reorder.** Rewriting physical order (causal order) for readability — hoisting a completed turn above a round-seal marker. Positions shift; anchors die. Physical order is causal order is cache order; presentation derives, never permutes.

**FM-17 — Rollback orphans.** GM rolls back to an old round: truncate-to-anchor is safe, but summaries/embeddings derived from the abandoned branch survive and reference events that "never happened" — amendment chains pointing at erased entries. Audit catastrophe. Rollback must garbage-collect all derivatives downstream of the rollback point.

**FM-18 — Cross-tenant cache oracle.** Shared radix trees mean cache-hit latency probes reveal whether a phrase was prefilled before — a timing oracle against hidden information. Partition cache per tenant wherever hidden-info integrity matters; eat the hit-rate loss.

**FM-19 — Unverified declarations.** Orchestrator asserts anchors; engine skips verification "for performance." One orchestrator bug poisons every subsequent request silently. Engine verifies boundary token IDs and the hash chain at O(1) per anchor; full verification on cold load and on any anomaly.

**FM-20 — Architecture blindness.** Sliding-window or attention-sink models change the economics entirely: anchors beyond the window are dead weight; sink tokens must persist regardless. Anchor placement must consult the attention architecture, not just token stability.

---

## Boundaries

- **Minimum anchor span:** ≥ 512–1024 tokens. Below ~256, page-table bookkeeping exceeds recompute cost. Provider breakpoint minima (commonly 1024/2048) bind harder than your own preference.
- **Breakpoints per request:** provider-capped (typically ≤ 4). Canonical allocation: (1) end of system + world rules, (2) end of the stable ledger-history delta-chain, (3) end of last sealed round, (4) start of live suffix.
- **Digest structure:** delta-chain appended per round; cumulative digest rewritten in place is forbidden (FM-7).
- **Seam window:** re-tokenize last ≤ 8 prefix tokens ∪ first ≤ 8 suffix tokens.
- **Verification:** O(1) per anchor per request; O(n) only on cold load or anomaly.
- **Telemetry tripwires:** anchor-tier hit rate < 90% in steady state → placement bug; routine suffix re-prefill > 25% of context → anchor starvation; any hit on a span flagged post-deletion → immediate halt and purge.
- **Eviction:** pin tier-1 (system/world rules) explicitly; LRU otherwise evicts exactly the highest-value oldest anchors. Cap the pin budget or the working set starves.
- **Concurrency:** single-writer per session, monotonic versions, optimistic concurrency (edit carries base_version; rejected on mismatch).
- **Replay:** log the anchor manifest per request (span hashes, position bases, model tags). Bitwise logit equality across differing batch compositions is *not* guaranteed — kernel reduction order varies. The contract is semantic equality; tests assert behavior, not bitwise logits.

---

## What must never happen

1. Serve cached KV for a span whose tokens **or positions** changed.
2. Reuse KV across a deletion boundary — deleted content must stay deleted, including latently.
3. Mutate a sealed span in place; amendments append or nothing.
4. Splice raw token streams across a seam without re-tokenizing the window.
5. Key cache by position alone in any session that forks.
6. Update digests, clocks, or any volatile field in place.
7. Seal a partially streamed or interruptible turn.
8. Let LCS/similarity matching drive reuse; contiguous token-level prefix only.
9. Share cache across model versions, quantizations, or tenants untagged/unpartitioned.
10. Rely on an anchor declaration that wasn't verified.
11. Retcon history on reveal — forward publication only.
12. Leave orphaned summaries or embeddings after a rollback.
13. Send a shortened prompt assuming invisible server-side cache without an explicit contract guaranteeing it.
14. Rebuild sampler state from anything less than the full logical context.
15. Permit physical reordering of sealed content for presentation.

The one-line summary: **anchors buy you O(1) change-detection, not immunity from physics — token identity, positional identity, weight identity, and deletion-cleanliness are four separate requirements, and violating any one of them silently is the failure that matters.**
reasoning:
Let me parse this problem carefully. The user is asking about a hard systems problem: "semantic-anchor checkpoints so an agent's context edit re-prefills only the new suffix, in the Ledger of Empty Chairs game world."

This is a technical question about LLM agent context management, framed inside a fictional game world called "Ledger of Empty Chairs." The core engineering problem is:

1. **Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: You checkpoint an agent's context at semantically meaningful points (not arbitrary token counts), so that when a context edit happens, you can re-prefill only the new suffix rather than re-prefilling the entire context.

2. **Re-prefill only the new suffix**: This is about KV-cache reuse in transformer inference. When you have a long conversation/context and you make an edit to it (e.g., tool result injection, memory compaction, branch rewrite), you want to avoid recomputing the prefill for tokens that haven't changed — you want cache hits on the prefix and only compute the new suffix.

3. **Ledger of Empty Chairs game world**: This is a fictional framing — presumably a game where there's some kind of ledger tracking "empty chairs" (absent entities? seats at a table? players who left?). The game world provides concrete constraints: state that mutates, deterministic simulation, maybe hidden information, etc. I should ground the answer in this world: the ledger entries, chairs, occupants, etc., become the domain objects whose semantic structure defines anchor points.

The user wants **edge cases**: failure modes, boundaries, and what must never happen. Concrete, exact, grounded.

So I need to do real engineering analysis of prefix-cache-aware context editing with semantic anchors, and enumerate edge cases rigorously. Let me think through the actual technical substance first, then map it into the game-world vocabulary so it's grounded.

## Core technical model

**Setup**: An agent has a context = sequence of blocks/messages/tokens. Inference engine has a paged/prefix KV cache (like vLLM's automatic prefix caching, or Anthropic-style prompt caching with explicit breakpoints). A "semantic-anchor checkpoint" is a position in the context chosen because the content *up to* that point is immutable-by-construction (append-only region), so any future context version either contains that exact byte-identical prefix or diverges before it.

**The invariant**: For a cache hit on a prefix P, the new context must contain P as an exact token-identical prefix. Any edit must therefore be structured as:
- Keep a maximal unchanged prefix,
- Then everything after is "new suffix" → re-prefill from the first divergence point.

**Semantic anchors**: Instead of anchoring at arbitrary token positions (which break mid-block), anchor at block/message boundaries that are semantically closed units: e.g., a completed turn, a committed ledger entry, a sealed round of the game. The anchor guarantees immutability: once sealed, the bytes never change.

**The edit operations** that occur in agentic loops:
1. Append (new turn/tool result) — trivially suffix-only.
2. Insertion in the middle (e.g., injecting a system reminder, injecting retrieved memory near the top).
3. Deletion/compaction (summarizing old turns, evicting stale tool results).
4. Rewrite/mutation (editing a prior message, correcting a wrong fact).
5. Branching (forking the context for parallel sampling or alternative plans).

Each operation interacts differently with anchors.

Now the edge cases. Let me be systematic. I'll enumerate along several axes:

### Axis 1: Anchor placement failures

1. **Anchor placed mid-mutable-region**: If an anchor is declared at a point where later content can still mutate (e.g., a ledger entry that can still be amended), then a mutation after the anchor invalidates the claimed prefix → silent cache poisoning if the engine trusts the anchor without verifying. Failure mode: the engine serves cached KV for a prefix whose tokens actually changed; the model attends over stale values; outputs are subtly wrong (hallucinated consistency). This is the worst class: no crash, just corrupted cognition.

2. **Anchor at a token boundary that isn't a tokenizer boundary**: Anchors defined by character offsets or message indices but the cache is keyed by token ids. If re-tokenization of the "unchanged" prefix yields different token ids (e.g., due to BPE merges across the boundary between the last kept token and first new token — the classic "token healing" / boundary merge problem), the prefix diverges at the last token(s) even though text is identical. Concrete case: prefix ends with "...ch" and suffix begins "air" — merged as one token "chair" in retokenization vs. ["ch","air"] originally. Cache key mismatch → full re-prefill (correctness fine, perf lost) OR worse, if someone naively splices token streams, corrupted text. Must never splice token streams across an anchor without re-tokenizing the seam window.

3. **Anchor drift under normalization**: If the pipeline normalizes whitespace/unicode differently on different passes (e.g., NFC vs NFD, trailing newline trimming), the "same" prefix hashes differently. Cache keyed on hash → miss; worse, keyed on index → collision with different content.

4. **Anchor too dense**: Anchoring every block means cache pages fragment; eviction pressure rises; you pay bookkeeping overhead exceeding recompute cost. Boundary: anchor granularity should be ≥ some minimum span (e.g., ≥ N tokens, or ≥ one sealed game-round). Below that, page-table churn dominates.

5. **Anchor too sparse**: One anchor at the system prompt end. Then any mid-context edit (compaction of old turns) invalidates everything after → full re-prefill of the whole tail each time. Cost blow-up exactly when compaction fires most (long contexts).

### Axis 2: Edit-operation × anchor interactions

6. **Insertion above all anchors** (e.g., prepending a retrieved-memory block after the system prompt): invalidates every downstream anchor. All cached KV after insertion point is dead. Failure mode if unhandled: engine computes attention with positional offsets shifted — cached K/V were computed with RoPE positions assuming old absolute positions; inserting shifts positions; naive reuse misaligns rotary phases → garbage attention scores. This is a real, exact failure: KV cache entries embed positional encodings; prefix reuse requires identical positions, not just identical tokens. So "re-prefill only the new suffix" is only valid if the suffix starts at the same absolute position index as before, i.e., insertions are forbidden anywhere except at the true end, unless you use position-independent schemes or recompute from the insertion point onward.

   That's a crucial boundary: **prefix-cache validity = token identity AND positional identity**. Any edit that changes the length of anything before an anchor kills that anchor. So the design must classify edits: append-only edits preserve anchors; length-changing edits (insert/delete) invalidate all anchors downstream of the edit point.

7. **Deletion/compaction below an anchor**: Summarize turns 3–10 into a summary block. Everything after the summary now sits at different positions. All anchors after the compaction point are dead. If the system naively keeps them ("they're semantically unchanged!"), you get the RoPE misalignment corruption again. Must never keep downstream anchors alive across a length-changing edit.

8. **Mutation of a sealed entry** (game rule violation): The Ledger of Empty Chairs presumably has a rule: sealed chair-entries are immutable. But what if the game master corrects an erroneous entry? Two options: (a) append a correction entry (amendment pattern — preserves anchors), (b) rewrite in place (destroys anchors). The design must mandate (a). What must never happen: in-place rewrite of post-anchor content while claiming anchor validity. If a rewrite is unavoidable, the anchor set must be truncated to before the earliest mutation, and the engine must be told explicitly.

9. **Branching/forking**: Fork context for two candidate plans. Both forks share the prefix up to fork point. Fine — both can reuse the shared prefix cache. Edge case: the two branches' suffixes are prefilled into the same cache namespace; if keys are (hash-of-prefix-tokens) they coexist fine; if keys are (session-id, position-index) they collide → cross-contamination where branch B reads branch A's cached KV. Must never key cache by position alone within a session that branches.

10. **Tool-result backfill**: Agent calls tool; result arrives; you insert it as a new message at the end — fine. But some frameworks insert the tool result *adjacent* to the assistant's tool-call message, which may require reordering messages (tool results must immediately follow tool calls per API schema). If the assistant emitted multiple tool calls and results arrive out of order, assembling them in arrival order vs. call order changes the middle of the context → mid-context edit → anchor invalidation cascade. Exact rule: assemble tool results in call order deterministically before sealing the turn; never seal the turn until all expected results are present; never let late-arriving results mutate a sealed turn.

11. **Partial tool results / streaming**: Result streams in chunks; if you seal the anchor when the first chunk arrives and then the rest appends within the same logical block, the anchor's "end" moved. Anchors must be defined as [start,end] spans frozen at seal time; appending to a sealed block is a mutation. Either don't seal until stream completes, or treat the streamed remainder as a separate appended block.

12. **Retraction/cancellation**: User interrupts generation; partial assistant output exists. Do you seal it? If you seal a truncated turn and later the "real" turn replaces it, that's a mid-edit. Rule: interrupted generations are marked provisional, never anchored; on resume, either continue (append-only) or discard-and-regenerate (truncate to last anchor — which is safe precisely because truncation to an anchor is the one length-changing op that preserves all upstream anchors).

    Actually truncation is special: deleting a suffix preserves all upstream anchors and their positions. Truncation-to-anchor is always safe. That's the one destructive op that's free.

13. **Compaction interacting with truncation**: Compaction = delete old + insert summary. Delete-old alone is safe for upstream anchors (they're upstream... wait, deleting old turns deletes things *below* the surviving anchors — the survivors shift down in position). Hmm: if you delete turns 3–10 and keep turns 11+, turns 11+ shift to earlier positions → their cached KV has wrong positions → dead. Unless the engine supports position remapping (some paged caches can't; RoPE is absolute). With relative/position-remappable schemes (e.g., YaRN-style adjustments or recomputing only position-dependent parts — but K/V values themselves depend on positions of the tokens when computed, since attention at computation time saw earlier context)... 

    Careful here: KV values for token at position p are computed via attention over tokens at positions < p. If you delete earlier tokens, the cached K/V for later tokens were computed attending to now-deleted tokens. Even with perfect position remapping, the *values* encode the deleted context. Reusing them means the model "remembers" deleted content invisibly. Is that a bug or feature? It's a correctness hazard: the model's behavior reflects context that's supposedly gone (e.g., compacted away). It can leak secrets/details that were "deleted." This is a subtle, important edge case: **KV reuse across deletions resurrects deleted content in latent form**. Must never reuse KV spanning a deletion if deletion was meant to remove information (privacy/secret-scrubbing scenario). For pure summarization-for-length it might be acceptable-ish but changes model behavior unpredictably. Grounded rule: any deletion boundary forces re-prefill from the deletion point; no exceptions, even with position remapping.

14. **Hash collisions / weak cache keys**: Keying anchors by (length, first-token-id) or short hash → collision risk. Two different prefixes same key → poisoned reuse. Use strong hash (128-bit+) over exact token id sequence plus position base plus model/quantization version tag.

15. **Model/version skew**: Cache entries computed under model v1 reused for v2 (fine-tune update, quantization change, sampler-state change like presence of logit bias?). KV is model-specific. Tag cache lines with model fingerprint. Must never share across versions.

16. **Quantization mismatch**: KV stored fp16 vs evicted-to-int8; mixing precision across a single attention span → numerically inconsistent attention. If suffix computed in fp16 attends to prefix KV in int8, quality degrades non-deterministically depending on what got evicted. Boundary: pin precision per session or accept whole-span downgrade.

17. **Sliding-window / attention-sink models**: If the serving model uses sliding window attention (Mistral-style) or streamingLLM sinks, prefix caching semantics differ: distant prefix KV may be droppable anyway, or conversely sink tokens must persist. Anchor scheme must know the attention architecture. Edge: anchors beyond the window are useless; anchors must align with window boundaries or you waste memory.

18. **Speculative decoding interaction**: Draft model caches differ from target. If draft-model KV is also cached by anchors, mismatched vocab/tokenization between draft/target breaks token-id-keyed sharing. Keep namespaces separate.

19. **Batching/radix-tree eviction race**: Engine evicts a prefix page between your "check availability" and "commit request" → partial hit. Engines handle this internally (vLLM recomputes missing pages), but if your orchestration layer assumed the hit and skipped sending those tokens (some APIs require resending full prompt anyway; others allow cache-reference), you get truncated prompts. Never send a prompt shorter than the full logical context relying on server-side cache; send full tokens, let cache dedupe — unless the API contract explicitly supports reference-based continuation, in which case verify the contract's staleness rules.

20. **The "empty chair" specifics** — grounding in the game world. Let me invent precise mechanics consistent with the name: The Ledger of Empty Chairs tracks seats at a table; each chair is either Occupied (an entity with state) or Empty (vacated, with a tombstone record: who left, when, why). Entries are append-only; corrections are amendments. Game rounds seal periodically. Agents (players/NPC minds) run on LLM context windows; their context includes the ledger digest.

    Game-world-specific edge cases:
    - **Chair resurrection**: An empty chair gets re-occupied by the same entity returning. Naive diff says "chair 7 = Alice" matches an old entry → tempted to reuse old anchor/digest. But the ledger semantics say it's a new occupancy epoch; the context must reflect return-as-new-event. If the anchor scheme dedupes by entity identity rather than event identity, it will wrongly treat the return as unchanged → stale context. Anchors key on event/span identity, never entity identity.
    - **Empty-chair tombstone amendments**: tombstone reason corrected via amendment entry. Amendment is append-only → anchors survive. But a summarizer that folds amendment into the original tombstone produces a rewritten past → mid-context divergence. Rule: summaries must be additive blocks, never in-place folds, else anchor invalidation.
    - **Hidden-information reveals**: A chair's occupant had a secret; reveal event publishes it. Pre-reveal context blocks contain references that are now interpretable differently — but text unchanged, so anchors hold. Good. But if the system "retroactively redacts" the secret from history upon reveal (some games do retcon), that's a mid-context mutation → all downstream anchors die, plus the KV-resurrection hazard (#13) applies doubly: reusing pre-redaction KV leaks the secret. Must never retcon; amend forward.
    - **Round seals as natural anchors**: Seal events are the canonical anchor points. Edge: a seal happens mid-tool-loop (agent mid-action when round ends). Sealing while the turn is incomplete creates an anchor whose following content (the turn's completion) will arrive later — that's fine (append-only), but if the framework then reorders the completed turn before the seal marker for readability, positions shift → invalidation. Ordering discipline: physical order = causal order; presentation order must not differ from physical order.
    - **Multiple agents sharing a world-ledger digest**: Each agent's context embeds a digest of the shared ledger. Digest updates each round → the digest block changes for everyone → if digest sits early in context (after system prompt), every agent re-prefills almost everything each round. Placement boundary: put volatile digests as late as possible (just before the live suffix), or maintain a stable "history digest chain" where each round appends a delta rather than rewriting a cumulative digest. Cumulative-digest-in-place is the classic self-inflicted full-reprefill bug.
    - **Clock/time injections**: Timestamps embedded per-turn are fine (each turn's timestamp fixed at creation). But a "current time" line updated in place each tick is a mid-context mutation every tick → constant full re-prefill. Never update-in-place; append ticks.
    - **Determinism/replay requirement**: The game needs replayability (audit of who-knew-what-when). Context versions must be reconstructible. If cache reuse silently alters effective context (via #13 resurrection or #6 misalignment), replays diverge from live runs. Requirement: log anchor manifests (span hashes, position bases, model tags) per request so any run is reproducible bit-exactly given the manifest. Must never have unlogged cache hits affecting behavior.

21. **Suffix-only re-prefill correctness boundary**: "Only the new suffix" presumes the suffix's attention over the cached prefix equals what a full re-prefill would produce. True iff: identical tokens, identical positions, identical model weights, identical attention implementation (masking, sinks), and no cross-request nondeterminism (batched kernels can vary reduction order → tiny numeric differences; usually acceptable, but for strict replay parity you need deterministic kernels or acceptance of drift). State it exactly: bitwise equality is not guaranteed across batch compositions; semantic equality is the actual contract. Tests must compare distributions/behavior, not logits bitwise.

22. **First-divergence detection bugs**: Orchestration computes the common prefix between old and new context to find re-prefill start. Bugs: comparing normalized text instead of raw; comparing message lists where equal-content messages appear twice (duplicate blocks) causing alignment off-by-N; using LCS on messages instead of longest-common-prefix (LCS allows non-contiguous matches → claims reuse across a gap → corruption). Must use longest common *contiguous* prefix at token level, not similarity or LCS.

23. **Cache capacity thrash**: Long game sessions exceed cache; eviction picks LRU; your oldest anchors (system prompt + early rounds) get evicted precisely because they're oldest and least recently used, though they're the highest-value reusable prefix. Mitigation: pin priority tiers. Edge: pinned entries starve the working set → suffix churn causes misses anyway. Tune pin budget; monitor hit-rate per tier.

24. **Multi-tenant leakage**: Shared radix tree across sessions could serve another session's prefix if hashes collide or if key omits session scope where content is identical-but-context-sensitive (e.g., a block containing private info that happens to match another user's block). Identical tokens are identical tokens — reuse is semantically safe for the model, but cross-session timing/cache side channels exist (someone can probe cache-hit latency to detect whether a phrase was prefilled before — known class of attack). If the game world has hidden info, cache-probing becomes an oracle. Boundary: per-tenant cache partitioning when hidden-info integrity matters; accept hit-rate loss.

25. **Anchors crossing API cache-breakpoint limits**: Provider prompt-caching often caps number of breakpoints (e.g., ≤4) and minimum block sizes (e.g., 1024/2048 tokens). Semantic anchors finer than provider granularity can't all be materialized. Map semantic anchors onto provider breakpoints: choose the ≤N most valuable stable boundaries. Edge: provider min-block means a 900-token stable region can't be cached alone; pair it with neighbor.

26. **Off-by-one at the seam**: After computing divergence point d, you re-prefill tokens [d, end). But attention for token d needs KV of [0,d); if you re-prefill starting at d inclusive but the engine's "prefix hit" covers [0,d) exclusive-exclusive confusion → token d computed twice (harmless-ish, wasted) or zero times (hole → garbage). Define spans half-open [start,end) everywhere; test the seam with a dedicated probe (ask model to quote its first and last context tokens; assert exact).

27. **Unicode/bidi and control tokens in game content**: Player names with RTL scripts, emoji, ZWJ sequences; tokenizer instability across versions for these; also special/control tokens (<|endoftext|>) appearing in user-supplied chair-inscription text → premature stop or token-stream desync. Sanitize/escape; forbid raw control tokens in ledger content; test anchors with adversarial strings.

28. **Very long single blocks with internal anchors desired**: A giant transcript block where you'd like mid-block anchors. Can't — anchors must coincide with block boundaries or you must split blocks. Splitting changes the message list shape → if any consumer depends on message count/shape, breakage. Version the block schema.

29. **Rollback semantics**: Game master rolls back to a previous round (undo). Rollback = truncate to an old anchor + append divergent continuation. Safe for anchors upstream. But cached KV of the abandoned branch lingers; if session later "replays similar" content, radix-tree may match the abandoned branch's tokens and reuse — semantically fine (same tokens) but watch #13/#24 concerns. Also: rollback must invalidate any derived artifacts (summaries, embeddings) built from the discarded branch, else ghost summaries reference events that "never happened" — in a ledger game, that's an audit catastrophe: the ledger shows amendment chains referencing rolled-back entries. Must never leave orphaned derivatives after rollback.

30. **Concurrent edits**: Two subsystems edit context simultaneously (memory injector + compactor). Interleaved writes produce a context matching neither's expectation; divergence-point computation races. Require single-writer serialization per session with monotonic version numbers; reject edits based on stale base versions (optimistic concurrency: edit carries base_version; apply iff current==base).

31. **Anchor manifest trust**: If anchors are declared by the orchestrator but the engine doesn't verify token-equality (trusts hashes), a buggy orchestrator poisons silently. Defense-in-depth: engine spot-verifies (cheap: compare token ids at claimed boundaries) or orchestrator logs full hashes and engine validates hash chain. What must never happen: behavioral reliance on an anchor whose verification was skipped due to "performance."

32. **Cold-start after restart**: Session resumes; cache empty; everything re-prefills. Correctness fine. Edge: persisted cache (disk) loaded with stale model tag or corrupted pages → validate checksums + model tag on load; on any doubt, drop.

Also worth stating the positive invariant crisply:

**Core invariant**: A context version V_{t+1} may reuse cached KV for span S ⊆ V_t iff tokens(S in V_{t+1}) == tokens(S in V_t), positions identical, model/precision identical, and no deletion occurred within or upstream-within-the-attention-reach of S since V_t. Everything else is re-prefill. Anchors exist to make the "no change" check O(1) and to give edits a vocabulary (append / truncate-to-anchor / amend-forward) that preserves the invariant by construction.

Edit grammar (what the system permits):
1. APPEND(new suffix after last anchor) — cheapest.
2. TRUNCATE(to any existing anchor) — safe, frees downstream.
3. AMEND(append correction block) — preserves all anchors.
4. COMPACTION(delete range + append summary) — invalidates all anchors downstream of range start; must re-declare anchor set; KV downstream must not be reused (deletion rule).
5. FORK(copy manifest, new branch id) — shares upstream cache read-only.
Forbidden primitive: IN-PLACE WRITE to any sealed span.

- Chair entry sealed ⇒ anchor candidate.
- Round seal ⇒ mandatory anchor.
- Tombstone/amendment ⇒ append-only by rule; the anchor system enforces what the fiction implies.
- Empty chair re-occupancy ⇒ new event id; never matched to old spans.
- Hidden-info reveal ⇒ forward publication only; retcon forbidden (both by fiction fairness and by cache safety).
- Shared ledger digest ⇒ delta-chain appended per round, never rewritten cumulatively in place.
